note: What the stored firms (circuit.json capture) spent in their latest fiscal year, from their audited filings, and which way Jev (TypeSafe System One) judged their money moves them. Money in USD billions; lobbying in USD millions (calendar 2025, Senate LDA filings); employees in thousands. direction holds the probability Jev put on each way (climb, integrate_down, expand_across, lean_on_state, harvest); defensive is 0 (investing for new demand) .. 1 (investing for fear of losing position); ai is the share of investment judged to go to AI (0..1). history holds each firm's fiscal years mostly in calendar 2015-2025 from the XBRL data of its 10-Ks on SEC EDGAR (SpaceX: its 2026 prospectus; every value's concept and filing are in Tools/corporate/history.json, the filings' folders in historyFilings), position is where the year sits on the time axis, and each year's judgments were made on its numbers alone (judgedOn), the latest year's too, so they differ from the firm's own judgment above only by what its words add. Judgments are model evidence, not measurements. economy holds the US totals the firms are set against.

direction.instructions: The economy can be read as layers standing on one another: raw materials and energy at the bottom, then manufacturing, construction and logistics, then services, with software, internet platforms, artificial intelligence and attention on top. Judging by where `company.name` put its money in `company.fiscal_period` (`company.uses_of_money_billion_usd`) and by what it says it is doing (`company.what_it_says`), which way is its money moving it?

climb.description: Moving up: its money builds a higher layer than the one it mainly earns from today, so it will sell software, platforms, data, AI models or access to attention rather than goods, labor or capacity
examples: a retailer building a cloud, advertising and AI business
a carmaker presenting itself as an AI and robotics company
a chipmaker funding AI model makers and software

integrate_down.description: Reaching down: its money buys or builds the supply beneath it, such as chips, data centers, power, factories, materials or logistics, so it depends less on suppliers
examples: a software company building its own data centers and power contracts
a phone maker designing its own chips and servers

expand_across.description: Spreading across its own layer: more customers, products or territory in the business it already has, or buying rivals, with no move up or down the layers
examples: an oil company buying another oil producer
a bank opening branches and widening lending
a drug maker launching new medicines

lean_on_state.description: Leaning on the state: its growth rests on government contracts, subsidies, tariffs, licenses or rules it helps shape
examples: a launch company living on public contracts

harvest.description: Harvesting: it returns most of its cash to its owners through buybacks and dividends instead of reinvesting it in the business
examples: a mature firm spending far more on buybacks and dividends than on investment

defensive.instructions: What drives `company.name`'s investment in `company.fiscal_period` (capital expenditures, research, acquisitions and stakes in other companies, in `company.uses_of_money_billion_usd`), judging by what it says (`company.what_it_says`): pursuing demand that does not exist yet, or fear of losing the position it has?
criteria: It invests to create or capture new demand: products or markets it expects to open, with no rival forcing its hand
Mostly to grow into new demand; keeping pace with rivals is a secondary reason
As much to seize new demand as to keep pace with rivals spending on the same thing
Mostly to keep up: rivals' spending or a shift in technology would erode its business if it held back
To defend what it has: it spends because falling behind in a race for capacity, technology or talent would cost it its existing business

ai.instructions: How much of `company.name`'s investment in `company.fiscal_period` (capital expenditures, research, acquisitions and stakes) goes to artificial intelligence: AI chips, data centers for AI, AI models and AI products, judging by `company.what_it_says` and `company.uses_of_money_billion_usd`?
criteria: None of it goes to AI
A small part: AI is one project among many
A substantial part, about a third
Most of it goes to AI
Nearly all of it goes to AI

firms.name: Mastercard

firms.name: Oracle
firms.strategy: Oracle says its capital investment program supports 'unprecedented opportunities in AI Cloud Infrastructure'. FY2026 capital expenditures were $55.7B, leaving free cash flow at negative $23.7B, and remaining performance obligations ended the year at $638B (up 363%). Oracle says it expects to raise about $40B through a combination of debt and equity financing in fiscal 2027.
firms.notes: Source: 10-K filed 2026-06-22, fiscal year 2025-06-01 to 2026-05-31. Oracle has no single cost-of-revenue line. costOfRevenue is the sum of three reported expense lines: cloud and software $17.60B, hardware $0.87B and services $4.56B. These exclude amortization of intangibles ($1.67B) and restructuring and other ($1.84B), which Oracle shows separately. capex is the cash-flow line 'Capital expenditures' ($55.663B, versus $21.2B the prior year); a further $5.28B of capex was unpaid at year end. Free cash flow was negative $23.7B per the earnings release. buybacks is 'Payments for repurchases of common stock' ($95M, versus $0.60B in FY2025 and $1.20B in FY2024). dividends is common dividends declared ($5.725B, $2.00 per share, paid within the year). The cash-flow line 'Payments of dividends to stockholders' is $5.79B and is not split between common stock and the 6.50% Series D mandatory convertible preferred. Oracle issued that preferred on 2026-02-05 for $4.95B net, and preferred dividends were $0.10B. acquisitions is null because acquisitions are combined with investment purchases in one line ('Purchases of marketable securities and other investments and acquisitions', $2.04B). Goodwill barely moved ($62.21B to $62.26B), which suggests no material acquisitions. Financing included $46.1B of new senior notes and term loans, and total debt was $129.5B at year end. netIncome is net income ($17.09B); net income available to common after preferred dividends was $16.98B. advertising is null because Oracle has not disclosed advertising expense since FY2022 ($273M that year). Employees: about 141,000 full-time (49,000 U.S., 92,000 international). Lobbying covers calendar 2025, not the fiscal year. It is the sum of Oracle Corporation's own 2025 LD-2 expense reports: Q1 $2.07M, Q2 $2.52M, Q3 $2.31M, Q4 $2.32M. These were filed under Method C (IRC sec. 162(e) definitions), which can include non-federal lobbying costs, so the figure is not strictly comparable with Method A filers. Twenty-six outside firms separately reported $5.07M of income from Oracle entities. That is not added, because LDA rules require a self-filer's expense total to include payments to outside firms.

firms.name: Chevron
firms.strategy: Chevron says it returned $27.1B of cash to shareholders in 2025: $12.1B of buybacks, $12.8B of dividends and $2.2B of Hess share purchases. Capex was $17.3B, higher than in 2024 'largely due to spend on legacy Hess assets' after the acquisition closed in July 2025. It achieved $1.5B of cost reductions in 2025 under a program aiming to cut structural costs by $3-4B by the end of 2026, while growing worldwide production 12% to a record, with milestones in the Permian (1 million boe/d), Guyana and Kazakhstan's TCO project.

Inc.'s own 2025 LD-2 expense reports (Method A): Q1 $1.94M, Q2 $2.14M, Q3 $2.03M, Q4 $1.85M. Three outside firms separately reported $0.88M of income from Chevron U.S.A. firms.name: Netflix
firms.strategy: Netflix says its first capital-allocation priority is reinvesting in the business, organically and through selective M&A. That means first its core series and films, plus live programming, its ads business (2025 ad revenue more than 2.5x 2024 at over $1.5B, expected to roughly double in 2026), games and new formats such as video podcasts. In its January 2026 letter it said it would pause share buybacks to accumulate cash for its pending all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros.
